title: The hypertrophy series: promoting progression in your training
summary: He argues progression is the most important hypertrophy variable for naturals: every lift should keep progressing in service of raising tonnage, not for strength's sake. Speed of progression matters less than direction, stalled tonnage explains many naturals who think they've hit their limit, and heavy compound strength saves time.

claims.claim: Progression is the most important variable for size; without it no amount of volume, intensity or clever programming yields results, and naturals can't grow without progressing.
Don't fall into powerlifting-style progression; the goal of lifting more is always to add muscle, otherwise it's a waste of time.
Progression should target raising your total tonnage, which requires a correct plan; the simplest method is adding weight to the bar.
No lift in your program should stagnate for more than about a month; all lifts should get stronger, not just the main compounds.
Progression speed differs by lift depending on muscle mass involved: deadlift progresses faster than overhead press, bench faster than curls.
Bodyweight and its fluctuations directly affect your ability to gain size (see his recomp guide).
Progression speed matters less than you think; bodybuilders shouldn't set strength deadlines, only physique deadlines such as a show.
Many naturals who believe they've reached their genetic limit have simply stopped progressing; their tonnage and lifts haven't moved in a long time.
A squat stuck at the same weight for two years is a roadblock: you can't grow legs without growing the tonnage you give them, and tonnage depends on the weight you can move.
He openly says he's weak, but his strength can still rise relative to himself, which raises his tonnage.
High-intensity training saves time: heavy compounds rack up thousands of pounds of tonnage quickly, so instead of many isolation sets you do a few squats and free time for other areas.
He doesn't promote aggressive lifting rotations because constant switching keeps you outside the specificity window needed for carryover, making progression harder.

Modern bodybuilding wrongly believes you can ignore the weight and level of exertion and just do high volume; high-volume rep ranges in irrelevant intensity windows don't drive progression or build strength efficiently.
